# Papal Inauguration of Pope Leo XIV

The **Papal Inauguration of Pope Leo XIV** was the formal liturgical ceremony marking the beginning of Pope Leo XIV's pontificate as Bishop of Rome and Supreme Pontiff of the Roman Catholic Church. Held on May 18, 2025, in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, the inauguration Mass formally installed Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost, who became the 267th pope and the first American to assume the papacy in the Church's 2,000-year history. The ceremony, officially titled the "Mass for the Beginning of the Petrine Ministry of Bishop Leo XIV of Rome," was celebrated with traditional liturgical elements and attended by an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 pilgrims, approximately 200 cardinals, 750 bishops and priests, and some 30 heads of state and other international dignitaries.

# Background

Robert Francis Prevost was born on September 14, 1955, in Chicago, Illinois, and professed vows with the Order of Saint Augustine in 1981. Before his election as pope, Prevost spent significant portions of his ministry in missionary work in Peru, including service in Chulucanas and Trujillo from 1985 to 1998, and later as Bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He was elected Prior General of the entire Augustinian order from 2001 to 2013, serving two terms, and was appointed Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops by Pope Francis in January 2023.

The papal conclave convened on May 7 and 8, 2025, following the death of Pope Francis on April 21, 2025. Prevost was elected on the fourth ballot on May 8, 2025, receiving more than 100 votes—exceeding the two-thirds majority of 89 votes required. White smoke emerged from the Sistine Chapel at 18:07 CEST (UTC+2), signifying the election of a new pope. After accepting his election, Prevost chose the papal name Leo XIV, at least in part to honor Pope Leo XIII and his legacy of Catholic social teaching.

# First Mass as Pope

On May 9, 2025, the day after his election, Pope Leo XIV celebrated his first Mass as Pope in the Sistine Chapel before the assembled College of Cardinals. In his homily, he preached against the lack of faith in the world and spoke of a church that would act as a "beacon that illuminates the dark nights of this world." He introduced his episcopal motto, *In illo Uno unum* ("In the One, we are one"), and requested that the Church's "first great desire be for a united Church, a sign of unity and communion, which becomes a leaven for a reconciled world."

# Inauguration Ceremony

### Date and Venue

The Mass for the inauguration of Leo XIV's pontificate took place on Sunday, May 18, 2025, beginning at 10:00 a.m. Rome time in St. Peter's Square. The choice of St. Peter's Square, designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini between 1656 and 1667, allowed for the attendance of large numbers of the faithful, as the plaza spans 320 meters long and 240 meters wide, capable of accommodating up to 300,000 people.

### Liturgical Elements

The liturgy formally began at the tomb of Saint Peter underneath the baldachin of the high altar of St. Peter's Basilica. Surrounded by the patriarchs of the Eastern Catholic Churches, Leo incensed the tomb while the choir sang *Tu es Petrus*, a motet composed by Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina in the sixteenth century. The Gospel was proclaimed in both Greek and Latin, expressing the unity of the Church and emphasizing that the pope serves both Latin Catholics and Eastern Catholics.

Pope Leo XIV delivered his homily in Italian, addressing themes of unity, love, and pastoral service. Drawing on the teachings of Saint Augustine and Pope Leo XIII, he emphasized that the Petrine ministry consists of "loving as Jesus did" and that Peter must "shepherd the flock without ever yielding to the temptation to be an autocrat, lording it over those entrusted to him." He stressed that Peter is called to serve his brothers and sisters and to walk alongside them in "fraternal communion, in the harmony of the Spirit, in the coexistence of diversity."

### Reception of Papal Insignia

During the Mass, Pope Leo XIV received two significant symbols of papal authority: the pallium and the Ring of the Fisherman. Cardinal Mario Zenari, representing the cardinal deacons and the order of deacons, imposed the pallium on Leo's shoulders. The pallium, a white woolen vestment made from lamb's wool blessed on the feast of Saint Agnes, symbolizes the Pope's role as the Good Shepherd and represents how he carries the Church upon his shoulders as the successor of Saint Peter and visible head of the Catholic Church.

Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, Pro-Prefect of the Dicastery for Evangelization of Peoples and representing the order of bishops and the Asian continent, bestowed the Ring of the Fisherman upon Pope Leo XIV. The ring, engraved with an image of Saint Peter the Apostle and the pope's name, serves as the pope's official seal and symbolizes his role as successor to Peter, the apostle called to be a "fisher of men." Leo appeared visibly moved during the moment of receiving the ring.

Cardinal Fridolin Ambongo Besungu, representing the cardinal priests and the African continent, recited a prayer for the pope before the imposition of the insignia. Cardinal Dominique Mamberti, the Protodeacon who had announced Leo's election from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica on May 8, was scheduled to impose the pallium but became ill during the Mass and was replaced by Cardinal Zenari.

### Rite of Obedience

Following the investiture of the papal insignia, twelve delegates representing the Catholic Church from around the world pledged obedience to the new pope. This addition represented a novelty compared to Pope Francis's inauguration Mass in 2013, which did not include representatives of the lay faithful in the rite of obedience. The delegates included clerics, vowed religious, a married couple, and young adults representing the three orders of the clergy, consecrated life, and the laity. Among them were Frank Leo, Archbishop of Toronto, representing North America; Jaime Spengler, Archbishop of Porto Alegre, representing South America; and John Ribat, Archbishop of Port Moresby, representing Oceania, each representing cardinal orders and continents.

### Conclusion of Mass

Before the conclusion of the Mass, Pope Leo XIV offered remarks in which he prayed for peace, specifically mentioning conflicts in Gaza, Myanmar, and Ukraine. The *Regina cæli* was then sung, and the pope imparted his final blessing. Throughout the ceremony, Leo used the papal ferula (crosier) commonly used by Pope John Paul II.

# Attendance

The inauguration Mass was attended by approximately 30 heads of state, 200 cardinals, and 750 bishops and priests, along with an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 pilgrims gathered in and around St. Peter's Square. Notably, U.S. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio attended on behalf of the United States government. Other notable attendees included Spanish King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, and Italian President Sergio Matarella. The presence of international leaders underscored the global significance of Leo's election as the first American pope.

# Papal Residence

Prior to his inauguration, it was reported that Pope Leo XIV would take up permanent residence in the papal apartments in the Apostolic Palace rather than in the Domus Sanctae Marthae, where his predecessor Pope Francis had chosen to live. This marked a return to the traditional papal residence used by predecessors before Francis.

## Subsequent Ceremonies

Following his inauguration Mass, Pope Leo XIV took canonical possession of the other major basilicas of Rome in a series of ceremonies. On May 20, 2025, he took possession of the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, where he venerated the tomb of the Apostle Paul. On May 25, 2025, he celebrated his second Regina cæli and took formal possession of the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, the cathedral of the Bishop of Rome, and the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, where he venerated the icon of the *Salus Populi Romani* (Protection of the Roman People). These ceremonies formally completed the installation of Leo XIV as the Bishop of Rome, as the taking of possession of these four major papal basilicas is a traditional element that emphasizes the pope's role as Bishop of Rome and head of the universal Church.

## Theological and Pastoral Themes

Pope Leo XIV's inauguration Mass homily emphasized several key themes that would characterize his early pontificate. He called for the Church to be a "sign of unity and communion, which becomes a leaven for a reconciled world," addressing the discord and division present in contemporary society caused by "hatred, violence, prejudice, the fear of difference, and an economic paradigm that exploits the Earth's resources and marginalizes the poorest."

Leo repeatedly stressed the inseparability of love and unity as the two dimensions of the Petrine ministry, drawing on Scriptural and patristic sources to articulate a vision of papal authority rooted in service and charity rather than power. He spoke of the Church's missionary vocation as requiring openness to the world and dialogue with other Christian denominations, those of other faiths, and all people of goodwill, seeking to "build a new world where peace reigns."

The pope's emphasis on ecumenism and interfaith dialogue reflected the legacy of Pope Francis while presenting Leo's own distinctive pastoral approach. In his remarks after Mass, he prayed specifically for the resolution of conflicts in Gaza, Myanmar, and Ukraine, demonstrating his commitment to the Church's advocacy for peace in troubled regions.

## Historical Significance

The inauguration of Pope Leo XIV represents a historic moment in the Roman Catholic Church. Prevost's election marks the first time in the Church's 2,000-year history that an American-born cardinal has been elevated to the papacy. His choice of the papal name Leo XIV, connecting him to the legacy of Pope Leo XIII and that pontiff's pioneering work in Catholic social teaching, signaled his intention to engage with contemporary social and economic issues through the lens of Catholic social doctrine.

The prominence of lay participation in the rite of obedience and the international representation among the delegates reflected contemporary developments in how the Church understands the participation of the entire People of God in the life of the Church. Leo's explicit commitment to unity, dialogue, and missionary engagement announced during his inauguration would frame the initial direction of his pontificate.

The Vatican has [confirmed](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/pope-leo-xiv-hold-inauguration-mass-may-18-2025-05-09/) that [Pope Leo XIV](https://www.elledecor.com/life-culture/a64716992/new-pope-leo-xiv-robert-francis-prevost-elected/), the first American pontiff in the Catholic Church's 2,000-year history, will be formally installed during an inaugural Mass at [St. Peter's Square](https://www.elledecor.com/life-culture/a64540229/pope-francis-funeral-plans/) this Sunday, May 18, at 10 a.m. Rome time. [Officially](https://www.exaudi.org/schedule-of-celebrations-presided-over-by-the-holy-father-leo-xiv-may-2025/) described as the "Mass for the Beginning of the Petrine Ministry of Bishop Leo XIV of Rome," the ceremony will be accessible to the public and marks the formal commencement of Leo XIV's role as Universal Pastor of the Church.

![Image 25: Conclave Elects The New Pope](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/ae123e90-0192-4f89-88e5-838fba1afd01.jpeg?crop=1xw:1xh;center,top&resize=980:*)

Dan Kitwood//Getty Images

The newly elected Pontiff, Pope Leo XIV is seen for the first time from the Vatican balcony.

St. Peter's Square (Piazza San Pietro), designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini between 1656 and 1667, spans 320 meters long and 240 meters wide, with a capacity to hold up to 300,000 people. The massive open-air plaza is framed by a colonnade consisting of 284 columns arranged in four rows. Atop the structure are 140 statues of saints sculpted in 1670 by Bernini's disciples. These colonnades create what Bernini described as "the maternal arms of the Church.”

The 69-year-old Chicago-born pontiff, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, celebrated his first Mass as pope in the [Sistine Chapel](https://www.elledecor.com/life-culture/a64539764/where-does-papal-conclave-happen/) on May 9, though that service was reserved exclusively for the cardinals who elected him.

![Image 26: Conclave Elects Pope Leo XIV](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/0851e3f4-710f-4671-867f-6b0d1aed6ac7.jpeg?crop=1xw:1xh;center,top&resize=980:*)

Antonio Masiello//Getty Images

Large crowds celebrate in St Peter’s Square.

The ceremony will feature the bestowal of the pallium, a white woolen band adorned with crosses symbolizing the pope's universal jurisdiction. This tradition has replaced the more elaborate papal coronations of the past—Pope Paul VI was the last to wear the traditional tiara.

Following his inauguration, Pope Leo XIV faces a packed schedule, including taking possession of Rome's three major basilicas: St. Paul Outside the Walls on May 20, and St. John Lateran and St. Mary Major on May 25. He'll also hold his first general audience on May 21 and meet with the Roman Curia and Vatican City State employees on May 24.

Who Will Attend Pope Leo XIV”s Inauguration?
--------------------------------------------

The inaugural Mass is expected to draw more than 200 political leaders from around the world. Notable attendees include:

*   U.S. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both Catholics, who will lead the American delegation.
*   European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen
*   Britain's Prince Edward
*   The Spanish royals
*   Argentine President Javier Milei
*   Israeli President Isaac Herzog
*   Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy

_This is the full text in English of the homily given by Pope Leo XIV in St. Peter's Square during the Mass of Inauguration of the Petrine Ministry May 18, 2025. The homily was delivered originally in Italian._

* * *

Dear brother cardinals, brother bishops and priests, distinguished authorities and members of the diplomatic corps, brothers and sisters -- I greet all of you with a heart full of gratitude at the beginning of the ministry that has been entrusted to me. St. Augustine wrote: "Lord, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you" (Confessions, I: 1,1).

In these days, we have experienced intense emotions. The death of Pope Francis filled our hearts with sadness. In those difficult hours, we felt like the crowds that the Gospel says were "like sheep without a shepherd" (Mt 9:36). Yet on Easter Sunday, we received his final blessing and, in the light of the resurrection, we experienced the days that followed in the certainty that the Lord never abandons his people, but gathers them when they are scattered and guards them "as a shepherd guards his flock" (Jer 31:10).

[**Read this next:** World leaders hear Pope Leo XIV condemn marginalization of the poor](https://www.ncronline.org/vatican/vatican-news/world-leaders-hear-pope-leo-xiv-condemn-marginalization-poor)

In this spirit of faith, the College of Cardinals met for the conclave. Coming from different backgrounds and experiences, we placed in God's hands our desire to elect the new Successor of Peter, the bishop of Rome, a shepherd capable of preserving the rich heritage of the Christian faith and, at the same time, looking to the future, in order to confront the questions, concerns and challenges of today's world. Accompanied by your prayers, we could feel the working of the Holy Spirit, who was able to bring us into harmony, like musical instruments, so that our heartstrings could vibrate in a single melody.

I was chosen, without any merit of my own, and now, with fear and trembling, I come to you as a brother, who desires to be the servant of your faith and your joy, walking with you on the path of God's love, for he wants us all to be united in one family. Love and unity: these are the two dimensions of the mission entrusted to Peter by Jesus.

We see this in today's Gospel, which takes us to the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus began the mission he received from the Father: to be a "fisher" of humanity in order to draw it up from the waters of evil and death. Walking along the shore, he had called Peter and the other first disciples to be, like him, "fishers of men." Now, after the resurrection, it is up to them to carry on this mission, to cast their nets again and again, to bring the hope of the Gospel into the "waters" of the world, to sail the seas of life so that all may experience God's embrace.

How can Peter carry out this task? The Gospel tells us that it is possible only because his own life was touched by the infinite and unconditional love of God, even in the hour of his failure and denial. For this reason, when Jesus addresses Peter, the Gospel uses the Greek verb agapáo, which refers to the love that God has for us, to the offering of himself without reserve and without calculation. Whereas the verb used in Peter's response describes the love of friendship that we have for one another.

Advertisement

Consequently, when Jesus asks Peter, "Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?" (Jn 21:16), he is referring to the love of the Father. It is as if Jesus said to him, "Only if you have known and experienced this love of God, which never fails, will you be able to feed my lambs. Only in the love of God the Father will you be able to love your brothers and sisters with that same 'more,' that is, by offering your life for your brothers and sisters."

Peter is thus entrusted with the task of "loving more" and giving his life for the flock. The ministry of Peter is distinguished precisely by this self-sacrificing love, because the Church of Rome presides in charity and its true authority is the charity of Christ. It is never a question of capturing others by force, by religious propaganda or by means of power. Instead, it is always and only a question of loving as Jesus did.

The Apostle Peter himself tells us that Jesus "is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, and has become the cornerstone" (Acts 4:11). Moreover, if the rock is Christ, Peter must shepherd the flock without ever yielding to the temptation to be an autocrat, lording it over those entrusted to him (cf. 1 Pet 5:3). On the contrary, he is called to serve the faith of his brothers and sisters, and to walk alongside them, for all of us are "living stones" (1 Pet 2:5), called through our baptism to build God's house in fraternal communion, in the harmony of the Spirit, in the coexistence of diversity. In the words of St. Augustine: "The Church consists of all those who are in harmony with their brothers and sisters and who love their neighbor" (Serm. 359,9).

Brothers and sisters, I would like that our first great desire be for a united Church, a sign of unity and communion, which becomes a leaven for a reconciled world. In this our time, we still see too much discord, too many wounds caused by hatred, violence, prejudice, the fear of difference, and an economic paradigm that exploits the Earth's resources and marginalizes the poorest. For our part, we want to be a small leaven of unity, communion and fraternity within the world. We want to say to the world, with humility and joy: Look to Christ! Come closer to him! Welcome his word that enlightens and consoles! Listen to his offer of love and become his one family: in the one Christ, we are one. This is the path to follow together, among ourselves but also with our sister Christian churches, with those who follow other religious paths, with those who are searching for God, with all women and men of good will, in order to build a new world where peace reigns!

This is the missionary spirit that must animate us; not closing ourselves off in our small groups, nor feeling superior to the world. We are called to offer God's love to everyone, in order to achieve that unity which does not cancel out differences but values the personal history of each person and the social and religious culture of every people.

Brothers and sisters, this is the hour for love! The heart of the Gospel is the love of God that makes us brothers and sisters. With my predecessor Leo XIII, we can ask ourselves today: If this criterion "were to prevail in the world, would not every conflict cease and peace return?" (Rerum Novarum, 21).

With the light and the strength of the Holy Spirit, let us build a Church founded on God's love, a sign of unity, a missionary Church that opens its arms to the world, proclaims the Word, allows itself to be made "restless" by history, and becomes a leaven of harmony for humanity.

Together, as one people, as brothers and sisters, let us walk towards God and love one another.

[Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost](https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/documentation/cardinali_biografie/cardinali_bio_prevost_rf.html), a former prefect of the influential Dicastery for Bishops, is a Chicago-born prelate with views close to Pope Francis who spent many years as a missionary in Peru before being elected head of the Augustinians for two consecutive terms.

Born on September 14, 1955, in Chicago, Illinois, Prevost entered the novitiate of the Order of Saint Augustine (OSA) in 1977 and made his solemn vows in 1981.

His educational background includes a Bachelor of Science in Mathematics from Villanova University in 1977, a Master of Divinity from Catholic Theological Union in Chicago, and both a licentiate and doctorate in canon law from the Pontifical College of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome. His doctoral thesis was on “The role of the local prior in the Order of Saint Augustine.”

His career in the Church has been marked by significant roles and achievements. After his ordination as a priest in 1982, Prevost [joined](https://web.archive.org/web/20160304191403/http:/augustinians.net/index.php?mact=News,cntnt01,detail,0&cntnt01articleid=483&cntnt01returnid=49) the Augustinian mission in Peru in 1985 and served as chancellor of the Territorial Prélature of Chulucanas from 1985 to 1986.

He spent the year 1987 to 1988 in the United States as pastor for vocations and director of missions for the Augustinian Province of Chicago before returning to Peru where he spent the next ten years heading the Augustinian seminary in Trujillo and teaching canon law in the diocesan seminary, where he was also prefect of studies. He also served in other capacities there, including as a parish pastor, diocesan official, director of formation, seminary teacher, and judicial vicar.

In 1999, he returned to Chicago and was elected provincial prior of the “Mother of Good Counsel” province in the archdiocese. Two and a half years later he was elected prior general of the Augustinian and served two terms until 2013.

In 2014, he returned to Peru when Pope Francis appointed him apostolic administrator of the Diocese of Chiclayo. He was elevated to Bishop of Chiclayo in 2015. While there, he also served as vice-president and member of the permanent council of the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference from 2018 to 2023.

During that time, Peru’s bishops reportedly played an [important role](https://aleteia.org/2023/09/21/future-cardinal-robert-francis-prevost-a-missionary-at-the-service-of-the-curia) in ensuring institutional stability during the successive political crises that led to the overthrows of successive presidents.

In 2020 and 2021, Prevost served as apostolic administrator of Callao, Peru.

Pope Francis [appointed](https://www1.villanova.edu/university/media/press-releases/2023/prevost-appointed-cardinal.html) Prevost prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops in January 2023, a powerful position responsible for selecting bishops, a position he held until Pope Francis died on April 21, 2025. On September 30, 2023, Pope Francis elevated Prevost to the rank of Cardinal.

During his first months as prefect, then-Archbishop Prevost continued to remain characteristically discreet in the media, but was reportedly appreciated for his ability to listen and his mastery of issues. _Aleteia_ [reported](https://aleteia.org/2023/09/21/future-cardinal-robert-francis-prevost-a-missionary-at-the-service-of-the-curia) that a French bishop who met him two months after he took office praised his “judicious questions” and his ability to synthesize, stressing that this first contact had left him with a “good impression.”

On key topics, Cardinal Prevost says little but some of his positions are known. He is [reportedly](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/02/world/americas/pope-candidate-cardinal-robert-francis-prevost.html) very close to Francis’ vision regarding the [environment](https://www.vaticannews.va/en/vatican-city/news/2024-11/climate-change-conference-latin-america-cardinals-rome.html), outreach to the poor and migrants, and meeting people where they are. He said last year “the bishop is not supposed to be a little prince sitting in his kingdom.” Prevost appears somewhat less favorable to currying favor with the LGBTQ lobby than Francis, but he showed mild support for _Fiducia Supplicans._1In a 2012 address, he voiced concern that Western culture promotes “sympathy for beliefs and practices that contradict the gospel,” specifically referencing the “homosexual lifestyle” and “alternative families made up of same-sex partners and their adopted children.” However, regarding the Vatican’s 2023 document _Fiducia Supplicans_, which permits non-liturgical blessings for couples in irregular situations (including same-sex couples), Prevost emphasized the need for national bishops’ conferences to have doctrinal authority to interpret and apply such directives in their local contexts, given cultural differences.

Prevost has faced some controversy regarding clergy sexual abuse although he has been defended in both instances.2The cases have drawn considerable attention because, as prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops, Prevost is responsible for applying the rules of Pope Francis’ motu proprio [_Vos estis lux mundi_](https://www.vatican.va/content/francesco/en/motu_proprio/documents/20230325-motu-proprio-vos-estis-lux-mundi-aggiornato.html). The papal decree can lead to the resignation of bishops found guilty of negligence, cover-up or mismanagement of abuse cases involving priests under their jurisdiction. The cardinal’s supporters stress his innocence and say the cases have been inaccurately and unfairly reported in the media.

The first case involves his handling of a sexual abuse case during his time as provincial of the Augustinian Province of Chicago (1999-2001), when a priest convicted of sexual abuse of minors was [allowed](https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/2/26/22302129/catholics-priest-child-sex-abuse-st-john-friary-james-ray-richard-mcgrath-hyde-park-augustinians) to stay at an Augustinian priory near an elementary school and continue functions as a priest until later removed, and then laicized in 2012. However, Prevost is said to have never authorized that particular situation, the priest was not an Augustinian, and it took place before the [Dallas Charter](https://www.usccb.org/topics/catholic-safeguards/dallas-charter).3The local prior, not the prior provincial, accepted the request of the Archdiocese of Chicago to give housing to a priest who had been accused, but he had not yet been tried or sentenced. The Local Prior who accepted to receive the priest was a professional counsellor with experience in the area of safeguarding. Access to the school was not so close as the articles imply. No incident of abuse took place while the priest was at the Augustinian residence. Sources say the journalist who covered the story in the Chicago Sun Times has a record of looking for ways of criticizing many authorities in the Church (diocesan and religious), and is said to be neither balanced nor objective in the opinion of many.

More recently, questions were raised about Prevost’s knowledge and handling of abuse allegations in his former Diocese of Chiclayo. Two priests were accused of molesting three young girls, with the allegations surfacing in April 2022 during Prevost’s tenure as bishop. The case has been a source of frustration for local Catholics due to its slow progress and unclear resolution.

Some accusers have claimed Prevost [failed](https://cruxnow.com/church-in-the-americas/2024/09/scandal-plagued-peruvian-group-pushes-back-against-vatican-inquiry) to [properly investigate](https://www.pillarcatholic.com/p/cardinal-prevost-never-investigated) the allegations and covered up for the accused priest, but the [diocese has firmly denied](https://www.ncronline.org/news/cardinals-former-diocese-denies-claim-clerical-sexual-abuse-cover) this, stating that Prevost followed proper procedures. They stated that Prevost personally [received and attended to the victims](https://zenit.org/2024/09/12/church-answers-false-accusations-against-cardinal-francis-prevost/), and reportedly opened an initial canonical investigation. He also encouraged the victims to take the case to the civil authorities. In July 2022, Prevost sent the results of the investigation to the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith (DDF) for review. His supporters stress that he has documents from the DDF and the Papal Nunciature in Peru which also indicate that he was not only attentive to the presumed victims, but that he did all required in Church law in following procedures set out for these cases.4The accusations are also said to be part of a deliberate attempt by a former Augustinian (later dismissed from the clerical state) who has deliberately set about trying to attack and defame Prevost for reasons that have nothing to do with the abuse cases. In the Peruvian Episcopal conference, Prevost was instrumental in the editing and publishing of the Guidelines for Bishops and Religious Superiors for the proper response to cases of accusation of sexual abuse by clerics (Líneas guía). He was the first president of the Episcopal Commission for the Protection of Minors and Vulnerable Adults in Peru, and was a member of the Commission until he was named by Pope Francis as Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops. Prevost organized a meeting of the presidency of the Peruvian Bishops Conference with victims of the group Sodalitium di Vita Cristiana, and accompanied numerous victims of abuse as part of the work of the Commission.”

However, in May 2025 [allegations emerged](https://globebanner.com/stories/671154673-report-critics-of-pope-favorite-prevost-received-150k-to-remain-silent) that the diocese paid $150,000 to the three girls to silence them. Described as “longtime public critics of Prevost,” the girls reportedly blame Prevost for covering up their sexual abuse by the priest.

The allegations, [reported](https://infovaticana.com/2025/04/30/la-mala-gestion-como-obispo-de-chiclayo-lastra-las-opciones-del-cardenal-prevost-para-ser-papa/) in _InfoVaticana,_ [described](https://globebanner.com/stories/671154673-report-critics-of-pope-favorite-prevost-received-150k-to-remain-silent) the Peruvian scandal, which was the subject of a national television report including an interview with the girls last fall, as the “stone in the shoe for Cardinal Prevost.”

Ahead of the 2025 Conclave, Cardinal Prevost was being promoted as a possible compromise candidate if leading candidates were unable to obtain enough votes. His lengthy missionary service in Peru allowed him to be seen as a more universal candidate than American which mitigated problems associated with choosing a pope from a superpower in his case.

However, there was speculation that he might be considered too young and too recently made a cardinal to be seriously considered _papabile_ with any significant chance of being elected. Continued questions over his handling of sexual abuse have also cast a cloud over his prospects.

Cardinal Prevost is a member of seven Vatican dicasteries as well as the Commission for the Governance (Governatorato) of Vatican City State, indicating how much Pope Francis trusted the cardinal and valued his administrative abilities.

**Pope Leo XIV**[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-2) (born **Robert Francis Prevost**,[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-5)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-10) September 14, 1955) is the head of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") and sovereign of [Vatican City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_City "Vatican City"). He is the first Pope to have been born in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), the first to hold either [U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_United_States "Citizenship of the United States") or [Peruvian citizenships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_nationality_law "Peruvian nationality law"), the first from the [Order of Saint Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Saint_Augustine "Order of Saint Augustine"), and the second (after his immediate predecessor [Pope Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis "Pope Francis")) from the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas").

Prevost was born in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago") and raised in the nearby suburb of [Dolton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolton,_Illinois "Dolton, Illinois"). He became a [friar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friar "Friar") in the Order of Saint Augustine in 1977 and was ordained as a priest in 1982. He earned a [Doctor of Canon Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Canon_Law_/(Catholic_Church/) "Doctor of Canon Law (Catholic Church)") (JCD) degree in 1987 from the [Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_University_of_Saint_Thomas_Aquinas "Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas") in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"). His service includes extensive [missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary "Missionary") work in [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") in the 1980s and 1990s, during which he worked as a parish pastor, diocesan official, seminary teacher, and administrator. Elected [prior general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_general_/(Christianity/) "Superior general (Christianity)") of the Order of Saint Augustine, he was based in Rome from 2001 to 2013, and traveled extensively as part of this work, including to the [order's many provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Saint_Augustine#Provinces "Order of Saint Augustine") and [missions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Saint_Augustine#Priories "Order of Saint Augustine") around the world. He then returned to Peru as [Bishop of Chiclayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Chiclayo "Bishop of Chiclayo") from 2015 to 2023. In 2023, Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the [Dicastery for Bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicastery_for_Bishops "Dicastery for Bishops") in Rome, and president of the [Pontifical Commission for Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_Commission_for_Latin_America "Pontifical Commission for Latin America"). Upon his return to Rome in 2023, Prevost was made a [cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_/(Catholic_Church/) "Cardinal (Catholic Church)") by Pope Francis.

As Cardinal, Prevost emphasized [synodality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synodality "Synodality"), missionary dialogue, and engagement with social and technological challenges. He has also addressed issues such as [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), global migration, church governance, and human rights, and expressed alignment with the reforms of the [Second Vatican Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Vatican_Council "Second Vatican Council") and the direction set for the Church by Francis.

Prevost's election in the [2025 conclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_conclave "2025 conclave") was unexpected by observers; he was a [dark horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse") candidate, with Vatican insiders believing the prospect of a Pope from the United States to be unrealistic given its status as a [superpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superpower "Superpower").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Rocca-2025-11)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12) In honor of [Pope Leo XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_XIII "Pope Leo XIII"), who developed modern [Catholic social teaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_social_teaching "Catholic social teaching") amid the tumult of the [Second Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Industrial_Revolution "Second Industrial Revolution"), Prevost chose the [papal name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_name "Papal name") Leo XIV—both to echo Leo XIII's concern for workers and fairness, and as a response to the challenges of [a new industrial revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Industrial_Revolution "Fourth Industrial Revolution") and [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-13)

Early life, family, and education (1955–1973)
---------------------------------------------

### Background and ancestry

Robert Francis Prevost was born on September 14, 1955,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Moral_Ant%C3%B3n_2014-14)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15) at [Mercy Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insight_Hospital_and_Medical_Center "Insight Hospital and Medical Center") in the [Bronzeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Metropolis%E2%80%93Bronzeville_District "Black Metropolis–Bronzeville District") neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, on the city's [South Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side,_Chicago "South Side, Chicago").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_2025-16)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Bosman_2025-17)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-18) He is of [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Colas-19) [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italians "Italians"),[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-20)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-21) [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaniards "Spaniards"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Gates_Jr.-2025-22) and [Louisiana Creole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_Creole_people "Louisiana Creole people")[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-23) descent.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Gates_Jr.-2025-22)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_2025-16)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-24)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-kim-25) His father, Louis Marius Prevost, was a Chicago native, having grown up in [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_Chicago "Hyde Park, Chicago").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-26) Louis's father and mother were immigrants from Italy and France, respectively.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-bosman2025-27)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Serra_2025-4)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vergun_2025-28) he later became superintendent of [Brookwood School District 167](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookwood_School_District_167 "Brookwood School District 167") in [Glenwood, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenwood,_Illinois "Glenwood, was also an educator, and a librarian, including at [Mendel Catholic High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendel_Catholic_High_School "Mendel Catholic High School").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Chicago_Tribune_1990-34)

### Early life and schooling

Known as "Rob" to his family and "Bob" to friends as an adult,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_2025-16)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Griffin_2025-35)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-36) Prevost was raised in [Dolton, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolton,_Illinois "Dolton, Illinois"), a suburb bordering the far South Side; [his childhood home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_XIV_childhood_home "Pope Leo XIV childhood home") was purchased by the Village of Dolton after he became pope.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-doltonhome-37) He grew up in the [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish_/(Catholic_Church/) "Parish (Catholic Church)") of [St. Mary of the Assumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Mary_of_the_Assumption_Church_/(Chicago/) "Saint Mary of the Assumption Church (Chicago)") in nearby [Riverdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverdale,_Chicago "Riverdale, Chicago"). His parents were practicing Catholics who were very involved in the parish: Louis was a [catechist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catechist "Catechist"), a teacher of the faith; while Mildred was an active member of the Rosary and [Altar Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_Society "Altar Society"), sang in the church [choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choir "Choir"), provided services for the church and went to daily Mass. According to Leo, what influenced him spiritually was his parents' faith, prayer life and [Marian devotions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marian_devotion "Marian devotion") ("My parents prayed the [rosary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosary "Rosary") together their whole lives everyday") and their mutual love.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-38)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Burack_2025-31) His mother would call him and his brothers to go to [Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_in_the_Catholic_Church "Mass in the Catholic Church") before school at 6:30 a.m., and told them that Jesus "is your best friend," and Mass "a way to find that friend."[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-39) Leo went to the parish [Catholic school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_schools_in_the_United_States "Catholic schools in the United States"), sang in the choir, and served as an [altar boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_boy "Altar boy").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_2025-16)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-40)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-42) Prevost has two older brothers, Louis Martín, and John Joseph.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-43) Prevost aspired to the [priesthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priesthood_in_the_Catholic_Church "Priesthood in the Catholic Church") from a young age,[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Griffin_2025-35) and would play-act the Mass at home with his brothers.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Tucker_2025-44)

From 1969 to 1973, Prevost attended [St. Augustine Seminary High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Augustine_Seminary_High_School "St. Augustine Seminary High School"), a [minor seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_seminary "Minor seminary") near [Saugatuck, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saugatuck,_Michigan "Saugatuck, Michigan");[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-45)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-46) his brother John recalled how, from the end of [eighth grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_grade "Eighth grade") on, and especially after joining the [Order of Saint Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Saint_Augustine "Order of Saint Augustine"), until their later adulthood when [leave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leave_of_absence "Leave of absence") allowed them to reconnect, Prevost was hardly at home or with their family.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Tucker_2025-44)

At the Augustinian seminary, he earned a letter of commendation for academic excellence, consistently appeared on the [honor roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor_roll "Honor roll"), served as [yearbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yearbook "Yearbook") editor-in-chief, and was secretary of the [student council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_council "Student council") and a member of the [National Honor Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Honor_Society "National Honor Society").[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-47)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-48) He captained the bowling team and headed the [speech and debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debate "Debate") team, competing in [Congressional Debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Debate "Congressional Debate").[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-49)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-50) Well-liked and highly intelligent, Prevost had a reputation for helping other students as a tutor.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-51) Out of several dozen who entered the school with him, Prevost was one of only 13 students in his class to graduate.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12)

University and early priesthood (1973–1998)
-------------------------------------------

### University

In 1973, Prevost was planning to attend [Tolentine College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolentine_College "Tolentine College"), an Augustinian seminary in [Olympia Fields, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Fields,_Illinois "Olympia Fields, Illinois"), as part of the order's pre-[novitiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novitiate "Novitiate") program, but it closed that same year.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_and_Winfield_2025-52) He promptly enrolled in [Villanova University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villanova_University "Villanova University"), an Augustinian college located near [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), where he earned a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") (BS) degree in mathematics in 1977.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Mervosh_2025-53)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-54) At Villanova, he took elective courses in [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") and [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"), read the writings of [Saint Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Augustine "Saint Augustine"), and discussed the work of theologian [Karl Rahner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Rahner "Karl Rahner") with other students.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12) He lived in the Augustinian [friary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery "Monastery"), and was remembered as "particularly committed... to missionary work," and being "the most community minded" among the students.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-55) Prevost also worked as a cemetery groundskeeper at Saint Denis Catholic Church in [Havertown, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havertown,_Pennsylvania "Havertown, Pennsylvania"), while studying at Villanova.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-fox29-56)

### Entry into Augustinians

On September 1, 1977, Prevost entered the [Order of Saint Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Saint_Augustine "Order of Saint Augustine")'s [novitiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novitiate "Novitiate") in the [Province of Our Mother of Good Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St._Augustine_in_the_United_States#Province_of_Our_Mother_of_Good_Counsel_\(Central/Midwestern_Province\) "Order of St. Augustine in the United States"). He resided for one year at [Immaculate Conception Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immaculate_Conception_Church_and_Rectory_/(St._Louis/) "Immaculate Conception Church and Rectory (St. Louis)") in the [Gate District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_District,_St._Louis "Gate District, St. Louis") neighborhood of [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri").[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-57)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-58)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-59)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-60) In the summer of 1978, Prevost spent three months in [Clinical Pastoral Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_Pastoral_Education "Clinical Pastoral Education") at [Abbott Northwestern Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbott_Northwestern_Hospital "Abbott Northwestern Hospital") in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Gomes2025-61)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-62)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-63) He took his [first vows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_vows "First vows") on September 2, 1978, and his [solemn vows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solemn_vow "Solemn vow") on August 29, 1981.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Moral_Ant%C3%B3n_2014-14)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15)

He returned to his father's native Hyde Park to obtain a [Master of Divinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Divinity "Master of Divinity") (MDiv) from [Catholic Theological Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Theological_Union "Catholic Theological Union") in 1982 and taught physics and math at [St. Rita of Cascia High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Rita_of_Cascia_High_School "St. Rita of Cascia High School") in the [Wrightwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrightwood,_Chicago "Wrightwood, Chicago") neighborhood of Chicago during his studies.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-FitzPatrick_2025-16)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Rich,_Dias_&_Horowitz_2025-64) As his [spiritual director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_direction "Spiritual direction"), a guide to the Christian life, he chose a [religious sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_sister "Religious sister"), Sister Lyn Osiek, [RSCJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSCJ "RSCJ"), the supervisor of his theological reflection class. She described him as "calm and steady... a person who was at peace with himself."[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-The_Making_of_an_American_Pope-65)

### Ordination and missionary work in Peru

On September 10, 1981, Prevost was ordained a deacon by [Thomas Gumbleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gumbleton "Thomas Gumbleton") at St. [Clare of Montefalco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_of_Montefalco "Clare of Montefalco") Parish in [Grosse Pointe Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grosse_Pointe_Park "Grosse Pointe Park"), Michigan. That same year, Prevost concluded his studies at Catholic Theological Union.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Meloy-66)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Moral_Ant%C3%B3n_2014-14) Prevost was [ordained](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_orders_in_the_Catholic_Church "Holy orders in the Catholic Church") a priest in Rome, at the [Chapel of Saint Monica of the Augustinians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_degli_Agostiniani "Santa Monica degli Agostiniani") by Archbishop [Jean Jadot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Jadot "Jean Jadot") on June 19, 1982.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Moral_Ant%C3%B3n_2014-14)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Scaramuzzi_2025-67)

Prevost earned a [Licentiate of Canon Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licentiate_of_Canon_Law "Licentiate of Canon Law") (JCL) in 1984, followed by a [Doctor of Canon Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Canon_Law_/(Catholic_Church/) "Doctor of Canon Law (Catholic Church)") (JCD) degree in 1987, both from the [Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_University_of_Saint_Thomas_Aquinas "Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas") in Rome.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15) During this period, he also learned [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12) His doctoral thesis was a [canon law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_law "Canon law") study of the role of local [priors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prior_/(ecclesiastical/) "Prior (ecclesiastical)") in the Order of Saint Augustine.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-68)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Immaculate_Conception_Church_Lafayette_at_Longfellow_St._Louis_MO.jpg/250px-Immaculate_Conception_Church_Lafayette_at_Longfellow_St._Louis_MO.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Immaculate_Conception_Church_Lafayette_at_Longfellow_St._Louis_MO.jpg)

Prevost spent his [novitiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novitiate "Novitiate") at Immaculate Conception Church in St. Louis, Missouri.

"Padre Roberto" joined the Augustinian mission in Peru in 1985, serving as [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_/(ecclesiastical/) "Chancellor (ecclesiastical)") of the [Territorial Prelature of Chulucanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_Prelature_of_Chulucanas "Territorial Prelature of Chulucanas") (1985–1986), as well as an aide to bishop [John McNabb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Conway_McNabb "Juan Conway McNabb"). Much of his work in his first year in Peru was focused on disaster relief following severe [El Niño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93Southern_Oscillation "El Niño–Southern Oscillation") rainstorms. [\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Moral_Ant%C3%B3n_2014-14)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Clarke-2025-69) In 1987, after defending his doctoral thesis, he was vocation director and missions director of the Augustinian [Province of Our Mother of Good Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St._Augustine_in_the_United_States#Province_of_Our_Mother_of_Good_Counsel_\(Central/Midwestern_Province\) "Order of St. Augustine in the United States") in [Olympia Fields, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Fields,_Illinois "Olympia Fields, Illinois"), and worked with the faculty of the Augustinian Novitiate in [Oconomowoc, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oconomowoc,_Wisconsin "Oconomowoc, Wisconsin"), before returning to Peru in 1988.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-70) During his time in Peru, Prevost met and appreciated the [Dominican priest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Preachers "Order of Preachers") and theologian [Gustavo Gutierrez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Gutierrez "Gustavo Gutierrez"), a pioneer of [liberation theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberation_theology "Liberation theology").[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Scaramuzzi_2025-67) He also learned and mastered the [Spanish language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") during this period.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12)

Prevost spent a decade heading the Augustinian seminary in [Trujillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trujillo,_Peru "Trujillo, Peru"), teaching [canon law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_law "Canon law") in the diocesan seminary,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15) serving as prefect of studies, acting as a judge in the regional [ecclesiastical court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_court "Ecclesiastical court"), and working in parish ministry on the city's outskirts, coming into contact with poor farmers and Peruvian [indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Peru "Indigenous peoples of Peru").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-71)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Clarke-2025-69)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Kathedralbasilika_St._Maria%2C_Trujillo%2C_Peru%2C.jpg/250px-Kathedralbasilika_St._Maria%2C_Trujillo%2C_Peru%2C.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kathedralbasilika_St._Maria,_Trujillo,_Peru,.jpg)

Cathedral Basilica of Saint Mary, Trujillo. As a young missionary, Prevost served in various roles in the [Archdiocese of Trujillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_of_Trujillo "Archdiocese of Trujillo").

He proved successful in the Augustinians' efforts to recruit Peruvians for the priesthood and leadership positions in the order.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-72) He organized support for Venezuelan refugees to Peru despite discrimination against the Venezuelans.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-73)

During the _[Fujimorato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujimorato "Fujimorato")_ era, Prevost criticized the actions of then-President [Alberto Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Fujimori "Alberto Fujimori"), placing special emphasis on the victims of the [Peruvian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Army "Peruvian Army"), especially the [Colina Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colina_Group "Colina Group"), during the [period of terrorism in Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_of_terrorism_in_Peru "Period of terrorism in Peru"), as well as on political corruption. In 2017, he criticized President [Pedro Pablo Kuczynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Pablo_Kuczynski "Pedro Pablo Kuczynski")'s decision to [pardon Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pardon_of_Alberto_Fujimori "Pardon of Alberto Fujimori"), and called upon Fujimori "to personally apologize for some of the great injustices that were committed".[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-74) His years in Peru gave him personal knowledge of political violence and inequality; at times, as a missionary, he traveled by horse on difficult roads to reach the isolated communities in the valleys of [Lambayeque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Lambayeque "Department of Lambayeque").[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-75) He also stood out as a defender of human rights of the population of the [Norte Chico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norte_Chico_/(Peruvian_region/) "Norte Chico (Peruvian region)") region against the violence of the [Marxist–Leninist–Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist%E2%80%93Leninist%E2%80%93Maoist "Marxist–Leninist–Maoist") guerrilla organization [Shining Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shining_Path "Shining Path").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-76)[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-77) However, Trujilio, the area where Prevost served, was not particularly affected by the Shining Path.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Clarke-2025-69)

Prior provincial and prior general (1998–2013)
----------------------------------------------

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/St._Thomas_Church_and_Convent_--_School_02.jpg/250px-St._Thomas_Church_and_Convent_--_School_02.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St._Thomas_Church_and_Convent_--_School_02.jpg)

St. Thomas School in Hyde Park, Chicago

In 1998, Prevost was elected [Prior Provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prior_Provincial "Prior Provincial") of the Order of St. Augustine's [Province of Our Mother of Good Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St._Augustine_in_the_United_States#Province_of_Our_Mother_of_Good_Counsel_\(Central/Midwestern_Province\) "Order of St. Augustine in the United States") based in Chicago, assuming the role on March 8, 1999.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15) In 2000, he permitted James Ray, an Augustinian priest, to reside at St. John Stone Friary in Chicago under supervision. Ray had been [suspended from public ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_/(Catholic_canonical_penalty/) "Suspension (Catholic canonical penalty)") since 1991 due to credible accusations that he had [sexually abused minors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_sexual_abuse_cases "Catholic Church sexual abuse cases"). Prevost's allowing of the placement of Ray in a friary at the request of the [Archdiocese of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archdiocese_of_Chicago "Archdiocese of Chicago") and close to [St. Thomas School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Thomas_Church_and_Convent "St. Thomas Church and Convent") was the subject of reporting in 2021, prior to his appointment to the Vatican.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-The_Pillar_2021-78) According to the Augustinians, "the location was selected because of the supervision the priest would receive."[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-The_Making_of_an_American_Pope-65) After American bishops implemented stricter rules in the [Dallas Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Charter "Dallas Charter"), Ray was moved to other housing in 2002.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-The_Pillar_2021-78)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Herguth_2021-79)[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-80)

Elected [prior general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_general_/(Christianity/) "Superior general (Christianity)") of the Order of Saint Augustine in 2001, Prevost served two consecutive, six-year terms until 2013.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-81) During his tenure as the global head of the Augustinian order, Prevost lived and worked in Rome, but frequently traveled around the world. It was in that capacity that in 2004, he visited Buenos Aires and met Cardinal Jorge Bergoglio, the future [Pope Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis "Pope Francis"), for the first time. Their early encounters are reported to have not gone well. Prevost later explained that at the time, he thought he would never become a [bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishops_in_the_Catholic_Church "Bishops in the Catholic Church") after Bergoglio was elected Pope in 2013, but has declined to reveal what they initially disagreed upon. However, they were able to reconcile their differences before Prevost left Rome for Chicago in 2013.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12) Soon after his election as prior general, Prevost personally oversaw the creation of a web site for the Augustinians.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-82)

From 2013 to 2014, Prevost served as director of formation at the Convent of St. Augustine in Chicago, and as first councilor and provincial vicar of the province of Our Mother of Good Counsel.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Vatican_News_2025-15)

Bishop of Chiclayo (2015–2023)
------------------------------

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Santa_Mar%C3%ADa_Catedral_-_Chiclayo.jpg/250px-Santa_Mar%C3%ADa_Catedral_-_Chiclayo.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Santa_Mar%C3%ADa_Catedral_-_Chiclayo.jpg)

[St. Mary's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Cathedral,_Chiclayo "St. Mary's Cathedral, Chiclayo") in [Chiclayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiclayo "Chiclayo"), Peru, where Prevost was diocesan bishop from 2015 to 2023

On November 3, 2014, Pope Francis appointed Prevost as the [apostolic administrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_administrator "Apostolic administrator") of the [Diocese of Chiclayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Chiclayo "Diocese of Chiclayo") in northern Peru and the [titular bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titular_bishop "Titular bishop") of [Sufar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufar "Sufar").[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-83) He was consecrated on December 12, 2014, at [St. Mary Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Mary%27s_Cathedral_in_Chiclayo "St. Mary's Cathedral in Chiclayo") by Archbishop [James Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Green_/(bishop/) "James Green (bishop)"), [Apostolic Nuncio to Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_Nuncio_to_Peru "Apostolic Nuncio to Peru").[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-84)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-85) On September 26, 2015, he was named Bishop of Chiclayo.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-86)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-87) As required by a 1980 agreement between the Holy See and [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"),[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-88) Prevost became a [naturalized Peruvian citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalized_Peruvian_citizen "Naturalized Peruvian citizen") before becoming bishop.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Rich,_Dias_&_Horowitz_2025-64) At the time of his appointment, Chiclayo was described as a conservative diocese, having been staffed by [Opus Dei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opus_Dei "Opus Dei") priests for many decades.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Clarke-2025-69)

Prevost developed a close bond with the diocese of Chiclayo, directing a special message to them in his first message as Pope, calling them "my beloved diocese", "faithful people" and "faithful church".[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Olmo-2025-89)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-90) He was seen as being "very faithful to the [Church's social doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_social_teaching "Catholic social teaching")" and organized relief efforts during calamities. He also supported projects in favor of Venezuelan refugees and encouraged vocations in youth groups, giving strong support to the seminary.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Beltr%C3%A1n-91) He helped victims of trafficking and sex workers learn new skills and trades, and invited them to spiritual retreats, while ensuring that volunteer workers have adequate training. He is remembered for his capacity to listen and have discussions with different groups before taking action, and working with institutions when facing controversial issues.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Rueda-92) He established a diocesan Commission on Integral Ecology and appointed a woman to lead it.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Olmo-2025-89) According to interviews done by _[The Pillar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pillar "The Pillar")_, people in the diocese described their bishop as having a "balanced" personality, a "calming presence", showing "great charity and great clarity" in doctrinal matters, and a competent administrator and bridge-builder open to dialogue and never hurtful, with "[apostolic zeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelism "Evangelism")"[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Beltr%C3%A1n-91)

Prevost as Bishop of Chiclayo in 2018, commenting on extreme poverty in the region (in Spanish)

On July 13, 2019, Prevost was appointed a member of the [Congregation for the Clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_for_the_Clergy "Congregation for the Clergy"),[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-93) and on April 15, 2020, he became apostolic administrator of [Callao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Callao "Roman Catholic Diocese of Callao").[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-94)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-95) On November 21, 2020, he joined the [Congregation for Bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_for_Bishops "Congregation for Bishops").[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-96) Within the [Episcopal Conference of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Conference_of_Peru "Episcopal Conference of Peru"), he served on the permanent council (2018–2020) and was elected president of its Commission for Education and Culture in 2019, also contributing to [Caritas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caritas_Internationalis "Caritas Internationalis") Peru.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Wells,_Olmo_&_Sullivan_2025-97)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-98) His presence in the permanent council of the episcopal conference was seen by Cardinal [Joseph Tobin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Tobin "Joseph Tobin") as "extraordinary for someone who was not born in Peru. Clearly, he has a broad degree of acceptance in the divided group."[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-99) Prevost had a private audience with Pope Francis on March 1, 2021,[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-100) sparking speculation about a new role in Chicago or Rome.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-101)

Prevost has been accused of covering up [sexual abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_sexual_abuse_cases "Catholic Church sexual abuse cases") during his time in Chiclayo.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Will_County_Gazette_2025-102)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-The_Jerusalem_Post_2025-103) In 2022, alleged victims of abuse in 2007 by priests Ricardo Yesquén Paiva and Eleuterio Vásquez Gonzáles said the Diocese of Chiclayo failed to investigate their cases.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-104) The [Diocese of Chiclayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Chiclayo "Roman Catholic Diocese of Chiclayo") stated that Prevost followed proper procedures, met with Ana María Quispe and her sisters in April 2022 to personally attend the victims, encouraged them to initiate a civil action, and initiated a canonical investigation, the results of which he sent to the [Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicastery_for_the_Doctrine_of_the_Faith "Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith").[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-105)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-106) The sisters stated in 2024 that no full penal canonical investigation occurred, and an investigation by [América Televisión](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A9rica_Televisi%C3%B3n "América Televisión") concluded that the church's investigation was not thorough.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-107)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-108)

In response the diocese of Chiclayo stated the allegations of the TV program were false, calling on it to correct its inaccuracies. The diocese said that the accused priest "never admitted" to the accusations, that Prevost prohibited him from exercising the priestly ministry and the priest transferred residence to his family's home. Prevost submitted the dossier to the Vatican, which gave a "pro nunc" decision or temporary dismissal. The diocese later reopened the case and sent it to the Vatican anew, and thus it remains "open up to now."[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-109)

Speaking to the Peruvian newspaper _[La República](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Rep%C3%BAblica_/(Peru/) "La República (Peru)")_ while Bishop of Chiclayo, Prevost said: "If you are a victim of sexual abuse by a priest, report it. We reject cover-ups and secrecy; that causes a lot of harm. We have to help people who have suffered due to wrongdoing."[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-110)[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-AFP_2025-111)[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-112) Journalist [Pedro Salinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pedro_Salinas_\(journalist\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pedro Salinas (journalist) (page does not exist)") ([es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Salinas_/(periodista/) "es:Pedro Salinas (periodista)")), who investigated and exposed crimes committed by members of the now-defunct [Sodalitium Christianae Vitae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodalitium_Christianae_Vitae "Sodalitium Christianae Vitae")—including sexual, physical, and psychological abuse—has argued that Prevost always expressed his support for the victims and was one of the most reliable clerical authorities in Peru, leading Pope Francis to select him as prefect of bishops. Salinas has written that some of the Peruvian clerics linked to the Sodalitium sought to attack and defame Prevost in retaliation for his role in the Sodalitium's dissolution by Pope Francis due to its sexual abuse scandals, as well as Prevost being near to [Francis's political theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theology_of_Pope_Francis "Theology of Pope Francis").[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-113)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-114)

Dicastery for Bishops and cardinalate (2023–2025)
-------------------------------------------------

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Procesija_s_pok._papom_Franjom_%287%29.jpg/250px-Procesija_s_pok._papom_Franjom_%287%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Procesija_s_pok._papom_Franjom_/(7/).jpg)

Cardinal Prevost (first from right) during the procession with the body of Pope Francis, April 23, 2025

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Cardinal_Robert_F._Prevost_at_the_Consistory_on_30_September_2023_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg/250px-Cardinal_Robert_F._Prevost_at_the_Consistory_on_30_September_2023_%283x4_cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cardinal_Robert_F._Prevost_at_the_Consistory_on_30_September_2023_/(3x4_cropped/).jpg)

Prevost during the Consistory in 2023

By the 2020s, Pope Francis had become close to Prevost and advanced his career.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Horowitz,_Bosman,_Dias,_Graham,_Romero_&_Taj_2025-12)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Bubola-115) On January 30, 2023, Francis appointed Prevost prefect of the [Dicastery for Bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicastery_for_Bishops "Dicastery for Bishops") with the title Archbishop-Bishop emeritus of Chiclayo.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-116)[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-117) Prevost expressed a preference to stay in Peru, but accepted the appointment.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-Bubola-115) He continued to be active in the Latin American and Caribbean Episcopal Council and participated in the council's meetings in [Aguadilla, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aguadilla,_Puerto_Rico "Aguadilla, Puerto Rico"), in May 2023.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Robert_Prevost#cite_note-118)
